catalog_quote: Five syllable types in Mankiyali are relevant for determining stress placement: {CV, CVC, CVCC, CVː, CVːC}. Stress in Mankiyali, based on native-speaker judgments, is weight-sensitive and unbounded in that the heaviest syllable in a word attracts primary stress regardless of its position in the word. Moreover, Mankiyali possesses at least a ternary distinction in syllable weight, as demonstrated by the data in (1). (1) {CVː(C)} > {CVC(C)} > {CV} (Paramore, 2021: 44–47) ... When syllable weight is neutral in Mankiyali – where all syllables in a word are of the same weight – primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (1a). As is evident from the scale, syllables with long vowels, {CVː(C)}, are the heaviest syllable type (1c), and {CVC(C)} syllables represent the middle level of the hierarchy (1b). new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded weight-sensitive stress: primary stress goes to the heaviest syllable in the word wherever it is (including the final syllable), on the scale long-vowel syllable CVː(C) > closed short-vowel syllable CVC(C) > open short CV (the 2025 authors hypothesize five levels CVːC > CVː > CVCC > CVC > CV); when all syllables are equal in weight stress is penultimate; when several syllables tie for heaviest, the rightmost non-final one is stressed. Stress is not lexically contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per both sources: every long-vowel syllable CVː(C) that lacks primary stress carries secondary stress; short-vowel syllables get secondary stress only to avoid a lapse of two adjacent unstressed syllables (thesis p.48 gives a separate secondary-stress scale VV(C) > V(C)(C) and flags these results as preliminary).
new_statements.exceptions: Thesis (pp. 43-44): speaker judgments vary on VV.VVC vs VVC.VV words, and VCC vs VC ranking rests on one compound ('a huge heap'), so those sub-rankings were left open in 2021; the 2025 paper adopts CVːC > CVː and CVCC > CVC as a hypothesis and argues its duration results support five weight levels. Compounds may deviate. Words bearing lexical tone were excluded from the stress analysis; tone-stress interaction unstudied.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress from native-speaker judgments on elicited words (thesis) and from tokens placed sentence-medially in non-focused preverbal position to separate word stress from phrasal/focus prominence (2025). The language also has a marginal binary lexical tone contrast (tonal vs atonal words, from loss of OIA voiced aspirates; low functional load) described separately (thesis sec. 2.3; Englert 2022 p.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Both Paramore sources describe Mankiyali (ISO nlm, glottocode mank1256; locally also called Tarawara / Trawara), spoken by c. 500 people in Dana village, Bandi Shungli union council, Mansehra district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; single variety, no dialect split reported. Note the language additionally has a marginal lexical tone contrast (low functional load), so a catalog row should read 'weight-sensitive stress; marginal tone' rather than plain stress language.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 (pp. 294-296): stress is weight-sensitive and unbounded; heaviest syllable takes primary stress regardless of position; default penult when weights are equal; ties -> rightmost non-final heaviest; scale CVː(C) > CVC(C) > CV (after Paramore 2021), authors hypothesize five levels CVːC > CVː > CVCC > CVC > CV; secondary stress on all non-primary long-vowel syllables, short-vowel syllables only to avoid lapse. Instrumental study (30 male speakers): duration the only robust word-stress correlate; focus prominence engages f0, intensity, tilt, formants too.
